newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Record high stocks, low prices stifle Asian petrol.
newsitem.headline: Record high stocks, low prices stifle Asian petrol.

text.p: Asian refiners are once again under pressure to cut petrol (gasoline) production as Singapore stocks hit a two-year high, depressing prices to a six-month low, industry sources said on Thursday.
"The market is so flushed with oil, there is a need to cut output," a refiner said.
Petrol prices in Singapore plunged to their lowest level this year with the 95-octane unleaded grade offered at $24.50 per barrel on Wednesday, the lowest since early October.
The gasoline yield is currently just around $3.00 to $3.50 per barrel more than naphtha, the feedstock used in its production.
This is far below the breakeven cost of production, which is around $4.00-$4.50. The profit margin in producing gasoline from naphtha in early March was around $5.40 per barrel, traders said.
Refiners in Singapore only switched their reforming unit to maximum capacity in late February after operating at 75-80 percent of capacity for most part of the second half of 1996, traders said.
Prices have slipped from just above $29.00 since early March amid high inventories in the region.
Singapore weekly light distillate stocks, comprising gasoline, reformate and naphtha, soared to 7.6 million barrrels in the week ending April 16, Trade Development Board figures showed on Thursday.
Refiners in Singapore said lower petrol prices were also squeezing profits from reforming, the secondary refining process that converts naphtha into reformate, a gasoline blending component.
But sources said Royal-Dutch Shell, the largest refiner in Singapore, is again lowering its gasoline production.
"There is no sense to push the system so hard," a refiner said. "There are just no buyers, and the market is flooded with supplies."
Traders in Singapore said stocks in Singapore have reached critical levels as supplies have flooded in from the Middle East, Thailand and South Korea.
South Korean monthly petrol exports were boosted this month by 400,000 barrels to 1.5 million barrels, traders said.
"In May and June there should be a spike in U.S. demand...that is the only market that can help us now," a Singapore refiner said.

But the outlook remained bleak as the American Petroleum Institute on Wednesday predicted gasoline supply in the U.S. would be more than adequate to meet peak summer demand, even if the most bullish growth forecasts were fulfilled.

The latest in a series of South Korean refinery expansions, Ssangyong Oil Refining Co, an affiliate of the Ssangyong Group catalytic cracker (RFCC) early this month and exported its first petrol cargoes.
The catalytic cracker produce mainly petrol from straight-run heavy gas oil (diesel) with the aid of a catalyst.
Regional demand has been weak despite scheduled refinery shutdowns for spring maintenance in Japan and Australia.
Instead, the market looked towards the U.S. for support. -- Singapore Newsroom (+65-870-3086)
